unmapped_findings: Product of strength and ductility for the 950 °C/1 h specimen = 21 GPa% (ultimate strength × ultimate elongation), from Table 1 (b0065, table_001).
The 950 °C, 1 h specimen shows continuous yielding (no yield-point phenomenon), like the other annealed specimens except the 700 °C one (b0035, b0061).
For specimens annealed at 900 °C and 950 °C, the work hardening rates are similar, but the 950 °C specimen snapped (fractured) earlier than the 900 °C specimen (b0035).

At 950 °C the ultimate strength and yield strength continue the monotonic decreasing trend with annealing temperature, while the ultimate elongation is past its peak (peak at 900 °C) and decreasing (b0037, b0060, figure_016).
γ phase volume fraction is about 57%–63% over the 900–1200 °C range, reaching the largest value (~63%) around 1000 °C and decreasing slightly to ~57% at 1200 °C (b0033, b0053).
Dissolution temperature of κ-carbide is between 850 °C and 900 °C (higher than the Thermo-Calc value of 823 °C); thus no matrix κ-carbide is expected in the 950 °C specimen (b0008, b0033, b0052).

In Table 2 the present steel (best condition, 900 °C) is compared with other Fe–Mn–Al–C steels; the present steel has the lowest ultimate elongation (36.6%) and the lowest product of strength and ductility (31 GPa%) among the listed steels. Note these comparison values correspond to the 900 °C condition, not directly to the 950 °C sample (b0071, table_002).

EDS line-scan elemental partitioning (κ-carbide richest in Mn and Al; γ richer in Mn and lower in Al than α) was performed only on the 800 °C and 900 °C specimens, not on the 950 °C specimen (b0032, figure_013).
